The Phantom of the Opera.text: On 11 February 2012 it became the first Broadway production ever to reach 10,000 performances.
The Phantom of the Opera.evidence: The Phantom of the Opera is the longest running show in Broadway history, and celebrated its 10,000th performance on 11 February 2012, becoming the first Broadway production in history to do so.

Chicago.text: It is based on a 1926 play by Maurine Dallas Watkins, a reporter who covered real murder trials in 1924.
Chicago.evidence: The musical Chicago is based on a play of the same name by reporter and playwright Maurine Dallas Watkins, who was assigned to cover the 1924 trials of accused murderers Beulah Annan and Belva Gaertner for the Chicago Tribune.

The Lion King.text: Julie Taymor became the first woman to win the Tony for Best Direction of a Musical.
The Lion King.evidence: including six Tony Awards, one for Best Musical and Best Direction of a Musical, making director Julie Taymor the first woman to earn such an honor.

Wicked.text: In the final week of 2024 it became the first Broadway show to earn over $5 million in a single week.
Wicked.evidence: In the final week of 2024, the Broadway production became the first to earn over US$5 million in a single week.

Cats.text: A purpose-built theatre in Japan has staged it more than 10,000 times since 1983.
Cats.evidence: as well as an ongoing run in a purpose-built theatre in Japan that has played over 10,000 performances since it opened in 1983.

Les Misérables.text: It began as a French concept album in 1980 before an English version opened in London in 1985.
Les Misérables.evidence: The show was recorded as a concept album, which was released in 1980, and then presented on stage for four months at the Palais des Sports. In 1983 it was adapted into an English-language version by producer Cameron Mackintosh and Royal Shakespeare Company directors Trevor Nunn and John Caird. This version, expanded and reorganized from the original, opened in London in 1985,

A Chorus Line.text: It won nine Tony Awards and the 1976 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
A Chorus Line.evidence: An unprecedented box office and critical hit, the musical received twelve Tony Award nominations and won nine, in addition to the 1976 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

Oh! Calcutta!.text: Samuel Beckett and John Lennon were among the writers of its sketches.
Oh! Calcutta!.evidence: Sketches were written by, among others, Samuel Beckett, John Lennon, Sam Shepard, Leonard Melfi, Edna O'Brien, Sherman Yellen, Jules Feiffer and Tynan, and often featured the cast nude.

The Book of Mormon.text: Co-writer Robert Lopez went on to co-write the songs for Disney's Frozen and Coco.
The Book of Mormon.evidence: After the success of The Book of Mormon, he later became known for co-writing the songs featured in the Disney animated films Frozen, its sequel Frozen II, and Coco, with his wife Kristen Anderson-Lopez.

Mamma Mia!.text: Producer Judy Craymer first saw its theatrical potential in the song "The Winner Takes It All".
Mamma Mia!.evidence: It was the song "The Winner Takes It All" that suggested to her the theatrical potential of their pop songs.
